pages.name: Kilifi New Year (Beneath the Baobabs)
pages.blurb: New Year festival on a baobab plateau on the Kenyan coast; about 4,000 tickets for its fourth edition, 2019–20.

pages.name: The Labyrinth
pages.blurb: Mindgames' techno weekend, its line-up revealed only on arrival in 2018, with a Funktion-One rig in 2019; Wada Tōge 2001, Naeba Greenland 2009–18, Minakami from 2019.

pages.name: Lord of the Mics
pages.blurb: Jammer's filmed MC clash series, begun in his basement with Wiley against Kano and released on DVD.

pages.name: Lovebox
pages.blurb: Groove Armada's festival, in Victoria Park until 2017 and Gunnersbury from 2018; Margate revival scheduled for May 2026.

pages.name: Mayday
pages.blurb: First on 14 December 1991; Dortmund's Westfalenhallen since.

pages.name: Megadog Midi Circus
pages.blurb: Megadog's summer 1993 tour of Orbital, the Drum Club and Aphex Twin, which Michael Dog calls Britain's first live electronic music tour.

pages.name: Movement / DEMF
pages.blurb: Hart Plaza, Memorial Day; founded free by Carl Craig.

pages.name: Mustache Mondays
pages.blurb: Monday party founded by Nacho Nava and Josh Peace at Crash Mansion; mixed DJs with performance art and built followings for Kelela and Kingdom.

pages.name: New York Cabaret Law
queries: "New York Cabaret Law" New York nightclub
pages.blurb: The 1926 licensing rule restricting dancing in bars, revived under Giuliani and repealed in October 2017 after a campaign by Discwoman's co-founder and others.

pages.name: Oasis Festival
pages.blurb: House and techno festival at the Fellah Hotel outside Marrakech, announced for 11–13 September 2015.

pages.name: Paraisópolis, 1 December 2019
pages.blurb: Nine people aged 14 to 23 died during a military police operation at the Baile da DZ7.

pages.name: Playaz
pages.blurb: DJ Hype's Playaz as a night: its drum and bass residency inside fabric's FABRICLIVE Fridays, halved with the bass nights after 2016.

pages.name: Rainbow Serpent
pages.blurb: Psytrance-rooted festival on open land near Lexton, Victoria, held on the Australia Day weekend from 1998; renamed Rainbow Spirit Festival in 2023.

pages.name: Rhythm and Vines
pages.blurb: New Year festival at Waiohika Estate near Gisborne, from about 1,800 in 2003 to a 25,000 sell-out in 2010; moving from Waiohika after 2026.

pages.name: Savage!
pages.blurb: Hip-hop night at Yellow hosted by DJ Muro and DJ Kensei, from 1997.

pages.name: Sensation
pages.blurb: The ArenA in white; trance as spectacle.

pages.name: Shangri-La (Glastonbury)
pages.blurb: The late-night area that replaced Lost Vagueness in Glastonbury's south-east corner in 2008, licensed until 6am.

pages.name: Solomun +1
pages.blurb: Solomun's Sunday at Pacha since 2013: one invited guest each week, long sets and a back-to-back finish, with the DJ booth moved down to the floor.

pages.name: STAX
pages.blurb: Danny Tenaglia's Brooklyn party, planned for 15 April 2023 on ten stacks: the Phazon system from Vinyl and Gary Stewart's GS-WAVE prototype.

pages.name: Subliminal Sessions
pages.blurb: Erick Morillo's midweek night, which moved to Centro-Fly after it was evicted from Champs; a Subliminal Night late in 1999 brought in Danny Tenaglia, Derrick Carter and Tony Humphries.

pages.name: Sunwaves
pages.blurb: Twice-yearly minimal techno and house festival on the Romanian coast; its 35th edition in May 2025 was its last in Romania.

pages.name: Temperance Club
pages.blurb: Dave Haslam's Thursday at the Haçienda, from 1986 to October 1990, mixing hip hop, rock and house.

pages.name: Time Warp Argentina, April 2016
pages.blurb: Five people died after the festival's first night at Costa Salguero; the city suspended festival permits and a judge ordered nightclubs closed.

pages.name: Trade Lite
pages.blurb: Second, lighter room at Trade, from about 6am, proposed by the Sharp Boys for funkier house.

pages.name: Twice as Nice
pages.blurb: Garage night where DJ Spoony was resident for more than seven years; it banned trainers, jeans and baseball caps and in time installed a metal detector to screen for guns.

pages.name: Ultra South Africa
pages.blurb: Ultra's licensed edition in Cape Town and Johannesburg; more than 40,000 in 2014, by Dancing Astronaut.

pages.name: Wake Up
pages.blurb: Laurent Garnier's Thursday night at the Rex Club from 21 May 1992, which brought Derrick May, Carl Craig, Jeff Mills and the founders of techno and house to Paris, often for the first time.

pages.name: White Party Miami
pages.blurb: AIDS benefit that began as one formal evening for 1,600 guests and grew into a week of circuit-party events.

pages.name: World Dance
pages.blurb: Lydd airport; the hardcore and jungle platform.

pages.name: YinYang Music Festival
pages.blurb: Rainbow Gao and Tommy Hendriks's festival on the Huangyaguan section of the Great Wall, about 1,000 strong in 2017.

pages.name: Entertainments (Increased Penalties) Act 1990
pages.blurb: Graham Bright's private member's bill: £20,000 fines and six months for unlicensed parties, and a large part of why the orbital raves moved into licensed clubs.

pages.name: The Goa noise ban
pages.blurb: India's Noise Pollution Rules of 2000: loud outdoor music stops at 10pm. In Goa enforcement came in waves, from a 2017 curfew to court-led crackdowns.

pages.name: The Night Czar and the night-time economy
queries: "The Night Czar and the night-time economy" London
"The Night Czar and the night-time economy"
pages.blurb: Amy Lamé, London's first Night Czar (2016), and the Night Time Commission. The post lapsed after 2024; City Hall proposed a Nightlife Commission instead (2026).

pages.name: The DTI's Radio Investigation Service
pages.blurb: The enforcement arm that raided pirate transmitters: 444 raids in 1988, 611 in 1993 and 928 in 1998, by ministers' figures.

pages.name: Ableton Live
pages.blurb: Software — Made in Berlin by Henke and Behles; loops, edits and resampling move from the studio into the set.

pages.name: Algoriddim djay Pro
pages.blurb: DJ app whose Neural Mix separated drums, vocals and harmonic parts on the fly from June 2020; supports Apple Music streaming.

pages.name: ARP 2600 / Odyssey
pages.blurb: Semi-modular — The other American synth: Herbie Hancock, Stevie Wonder, and the sawtooth leads of early electro.

pages.name: Bozak CMA-10-2DL
pages.blurb: Rudy Bozak's six-input rotary stereo mixer with headphone cue, the mixer at Studio 54 and the Paradise Garage.

pages.name: Pioneer CDJ-2000 / CDJ-2000 Nexus
pages.blurb: The 2009 deck that moved DJs to USB sticks, with a 6.1-inch screen and Pro DJ Link; the 2012 Nexus added Beat Sync.

pages.name: Pioneer CDJ-500
pages.blurb: The deck Pioneer counts as its first CDJ: top-loading, with jog wheel, cue button, loop and Master Tempo; £799 in 1994.

pages.name: Denon DN-2000F
pages.blurb: Two-piece rack-mounted twin CD player with pitch bend; £851.05 in 1994, when The Mix called it something of an industry standard.

pages.name: Pioneer DJM-500 / DJM-600
pages.blurb: Pioneer's first mixers: four upright channels, built-in effects and an automatic BPM counter, then a sampler on the DJM-600 of 1998.

pages.name: E&S DJR400
pages.blurb: Jerôme Barbé's hand-built portable rotary mixer, conceived with DJ Deep, Kerri Chandler and Joe Claussell; no more than a hundred a year in 2019.

pages.name: FruityLoops / FL Studio
pages.blurb: Software — Image-Line's Belgian step sequencer (1997): cheap, pirated and quick, the first DAW of grime, early dubstep and EDM's bedroom stars.

pages.name: Impulse Tracker
pages.blurb: Jeffrey Lim's PC tracker, with resonant filters and New Note Actions, the rival of FastTracker 2.

pages.name: Korg Kaoss Pad
pages.blurb: Korg's effects unit played with a finger on an X–Y touch pad, with a phono input and sampling, promoted to DJs from 1999.

pages.name: Logic Pro
pages.blurb: Sequencer from C-Lab's Creator and Notator through Emagic, bought by Apple in July 2002, $199.99 from 2011.

pages.name: Roland MC-202 / MC-4
pages.blurb: Sequencer — Roland's step sequencers, with notes, gates and accents typed in one at a time, the way the boxes were programmed before the computer.

pages.name: MP3, Beatport, SoundCloud
pages.blurb: Format — The record shop goes online: Discogs (2000) for the past, Beatport (2004) for new tracks as MP3s, SoundCloud (2007) for everyone's uploads.

pages.name: Clavia Nord Lead
pages.blurb: Virtual-analogue synth — The red keyboard from Clavia, who coined "virtual analogue": digital models of analogue circuits, the lead and stab of the late 1990s.

pages.name: Pioneer CMX-5000 / CMX-3000
pages.blurb: Pioneer's rack-mounted twin CD players; the CMX-5000's Auto Mix analysed two tracks and blended them, a precursor of sync by Pioneer's account.

pages.name: Polyend Tracker
pages.blurb: Polyend's self-contained, USB-powered hardware tracker of 2020, with the functions of a software tracker.

pages.name: Rane TTM 54 / TTM 56
pages.blurb: Rane's turntablist mixers, asked for by New York battle DJs; the TTM 56 of 2001 introduced Rick Jeffs's non-contact magnetic fader.

pages.name: rekordbox
pages.blurb: Pioneer's music-preparation software, first written with Mixvibes and bundled with the CDJ-2000; analyses tempo, beat grid and waveform.

pages.name: The sampler (Akai S900/S950, 1986–)
pages.blurb: Sampler — Cheap sampling: the breakbeat, the vocal stab and the piano loop of hardcore all come from it.

pages.name: Sonic Pi
pages.blurb: Sam Aaron's free live-coding program, made at Cambridge with the Raspberry Pi Foundation for school lessons.

pages.name: Stanton 681 / 500AL
pages.blurb: Stanton's calibrated 681SE and tougher 500AL, sold to discos for back-cueing; over half of the cartridges named in Billboard's 1978 and 1979 disco polls.

pages.name: Suno
pages.blurb: AI song generator sued by major labels in June 2024; Warner settled in 2025, Sony and Universal sued again in 2026.

pages.name: Technics SL-1200 / pitch control
pages.blurb: Record deck — The turntable with a pitch slider: beat-matching, the long mix, the DJ as instrumentalist.

pages.name: Thorens TD-124 / TD-125
pages.blurb: The TD-124 was in Alex Rosner's first club booth; its belt-drive successor of 1968 was the deck of The Loft and the Paradise Garage.

pages.name: Roland TR-808
pages.blurb: Drum machine — Built by Roland for lounge bands; the boom of electro, hip-hop and acid house. Discontinued 1983, cheap by 1985.

pages.name: Turbosound Flashlight and Floodlight
pages.blurb: Narrow-beam touring system (1989 by Andrews, 1990 by Turbosound) with a 12-inch, 6.5-inch and 1-inch high pack over 21-inch bass, and its wider 50-degree sibling.

pages.name: Vestax PMC-05 Pro
pages.blurb: The two-channel scratch mixer Toshi Nakama developed with Shortkut, Rhettmatic, Q-Bert and Mix Master Mike, with an adjustable crossfader slope.

pages.name: Allen & Heath Xone:3D
pages.blurb: Four-channel DJ mixer, USB sound card and MIDI surface in one box; Hawtin and Liebing consulted; £1,645 in 2006.

pages.name: Club Cultures (Sarah Thornton)
pages.blurb: Sarah Thornton's study of clubs and raves from 1988 to 1992, which introduced the idea of subcultural capital.

pages.name: Pink Noises (Tara Rodgers)
pages.blurb: Duke University Press book of twenty-four interviews with women in electronic music and sound.

pages.name: DJ Mag
pages.blurb: The Top 100 DJs poll, since 1993, that made and measured the superstar DJ.

pages.name: Frontpage
pages.blurb: Berlin's free techno magazine: the Love Parade's house journal, Tresor and the Mayday years.

pages.name: Last Night a DJ Saved My Life
queries: "Last Night a DJ Saved My Life"
pages.blurb: Brewster and Broughton's 1999 history of the DJ, revised 2022; with Collin's Altered State and Garratt's Adventures in Wonderland, the shelf behind this book.

pages.name: The Manual (How to Have a Number One the Easy Way)
pages.blurb: The Timelords' 1988 guide to making a number-one single with no money, written after "Doctorin' the Tardis".

pages.name: 23rd Precinct
pages.blurb: Bath Street basement that Billy Kiltie turned into Glasgow's house and techno counter, and the home of the Limbo label.

pages.name: Big Apple Records
pages.blurb: Surrey Street, Croydon shop with Artwork's studio on its second floor; Hatcha served, and its label was first to sign Skream and Benga.

pages.name: Clone
pages.blurb: Serge Verschuur's Rotterdam shop and label.

pages.name: Delirium Records
pages.blurb: Frankfurt's techno shop, the counter behind the city's 1990s scene.

pages.name: Eastern Bloc
pages.blurb: Afflecks Palace then Oldham Street: Manchester's dance shop, the source of 808 State and the Creed label.

pages.name: Halcyon
pages.blurb: Shawn Schwartz's Brooklyn dance shop: Smith Street from 1999, Dumbo from 2004, beside the club Output from 2016; shut in 2020.

pages.name: Importes Etc.
pages.blurb: The shop where Frankie Knuckles's Warehouse records were sold under a sign that said "house music"; one origin of the word.

pages.name: Love Vinyl
pages.blurb: Hackney shop at 5 Pearson Street founded by Zafar Chwodry of Reckless with Jake Holloway, Stuart Patterson and James Manero.

pages.name: Music Man
pages.blurb: DJ shop at Steendam 72 that sold ten thousand records a week in the 1990s; Renaat Vandepapeliere of R&S started out there.

pages.name: Rat Records
pages.blurb: Camberwell second-hand shop at 348 Camberwell New Road, Tom Fisher's from 1999, with a queue for new stock each Saturday; it closed in June 2022.

pages.name: Rooted Records
pages.blurb: Gloucester Road dance shop managed by Tom Ford (Peverelist), from which the Idle Hands label was run; it closed in 2010.

pages.name: Satellite Records
pages.blurb: Bowery shop that stocked every dance genre on twelve-inch and moved south of Houston Street about 2001; closed later that decade.

pages.name: Submerge and Somewhere in Detroit
queries: "Submerge and Somewhere in Detroit" Detroit record shop
pages.blurb: Underground Resistance's distributor, founded 1992, and its basement shop at 3000 East Grand Boulevard, beside the Exhibit 3000 techno museum.

pages.name: Unity Records
pages.blurb: Beak Street, Soho: Red Records' successor, selling rave, jungle, house and garage; managed by Seamus Haji.

pages.name: Warp Records (shop)
pages.blurb: The Division Street shop that became the label: Rob Mitchell and Steve Beckett behind the counter.

pages.name: All Systems and the Kamikaze rig
queries: "All Systems and the Kamikaze rig" Nottingham
pages.blurb: Alliance of Midlands and northern sound systems that fought the Criminal Justice Bill and bought a communal rig that could be lost to seizure.

pages.name: Channel One Sound System
pages.blurb: Mikey Dread and Jah T's east London roots sound, taken on from their father in 1979; at Notting Hill Carnival every year since 1983.

pages.name: Despacio
pages.blurb: James Murphy and Soulwax's vinyl-only night on seven 11-foot McIntosh-powered stacks, first heard in Manchester in 2013: hi-fi sound built for dancers.

pages.name: Eskimo Noise
pages.blurb: Neil Johannessen's Elephant and Castle sound company: Nexo and Crown rigs for World Dance, Moondance and Metalheadz at the Blue Note.

pages.name: KV2 Audio
pages.blurb: Loudspeaker maker with a factory in Czechia; its SL412 and VHD subs replaced Martin Audio in Ministry of Sound's Box in a refit from 7 January 2026, by KV2's announcement.

pages.name: Meyer Sound
pages.blurb: John and Helen Meyer's Californian firm: self-powered systems from the MSL-4 (1994), the PSW-6 cardioid sub (1998), the M3D array (2001).

pages.name: Sinai Sound System
pages.blurb: Huw Williams's system, begun with three bass boxes after an apprenticeship with Iration Steppas; about fifty by 2018.

pages.name: Studt-Akustik
pages.blurb: Peter Studt's Dresden hi-fi company; fitted Panorama Bar with a four-point linear array and six more subwoofers in 2017.

pages.name: Void Acoustics
pages.blurb: Rog Mogale and Alex Skan's speaker firm, founded 2002, now in Poole: sculpted Air Motion and Incubus designs, and systems for DC10, Tresor, Eden and festivals.

pages.name: Don FM
pages.blurb: South London's hardcore and jungle pirate of 1992–97, on 105.7 FM from Wandsworth, and the first airtime for DJ Trace and Ed Rush.

pages.name: Fantasy FM
pages.blurb: Techno, house and hardcore across the capital.

pages.name: Rinse FM
pages.blurb: Garage, grime, dubstep; a licence in 2010.

pages.name: Weekend Rush
pages.blurb: One of the earliest jungle pirates, broadcasting at weekends from Hackney's Nightingale Estate; a July 1993 raid made it the face of the panic.
